title: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)
hook: each tribal leader brings an identical gift, and each is listed in full

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Kohanim, the priests' three lines, and your line was bless thee, and keep thee. Did someone hear one sentence of good from you? Today, the end of Naso. Day four hundred forty.

At a graduation, the dean reads every single name. Three hundred students, and each one walks across the stage, shakes the same hand, takes the same rolled-up paper. It takes forever. Somebody in the back row checks their phone. Wouldn't it be faster to say: and congratulations to everyone? Faster, sure. But ask any parent in the audience whether it's the same. Numbers chapter seven makes the slow choice, on purpose, twelve times in a row, and the chapter grows long because of it.
screen: `EVERY NAME READ ALOUD.` → `THE SAME HANDSHAKE, 300 TIMES.` → `THE SLOW CHOICE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The Tabernacle is finished and anointed. Now the leaders of the twelve tribes come forward to dedicate the altar. Each leader is called a nasi, from the same root as naso: one who is lifted up. They bring their gifts one per day, for twelve days. On the first day, Nachshon, of Judah: one silver dish, one silver basin, both full of fine flour mixed with oil; one golden pan full of incense; a bull, a ram, a lamb, a goat, and more for the peace offerings. On the second day, the leader of Issachar brings exactly the same. And the third day, the same. Down to the shekel. And the Torah writes it out every time. Twelve paragraphs, almost word for word, then a grand total at the end. Eighty-nine verses. An editor might cut it. The commentators asked why it stays. Nachmanides answers that God wanted to honor each leader equally. Each one chose to bring the gift, each on his own day, and the Torah wouldn't let anyone be summarized as the same as the one before. A midrash goes further: even though the gifts were identical, each leader had his own meaning in mind, tied to his own tribe's story. Same silver, different hearts. This chapter is also read in synagogue during Hanukkah, because its theme is dedication. The Hebrew for dedication of the altar is chanukat hamizbe'ach. Hanukkah is the same word.
screen: `NASI: ONE LIFTED UP.` · `TWELVE DAYS, ONE IDENTICAL GIFT.` · `EACH ONE WRITTEN OUT IN FULL.` · `SAME SILVER, DIFFERENT HEARTS.` · then, large: `EACH GIFT COUNTED IN FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor the same good act done by many. Breathe, and think of a good thing that lots of people around you do, so often it blurs: the parents who all pack lunches, the nurses who all work the night shift, the volunteers who all show up on Sunday. Now pick out one of them. Give them their own paragraph in your mind: their name, their face, the way they do it. Then another. Don't summarize. The bell holds the time.
Naso, the portion of lifting, closing with twelve identical gifts, each one written out in full.
Your line: each gift counted in full. Today, where you'd write thanks, everyone, write out each name instead. Day four hundred forty.

trapdoor: what you thought: Numbers 7 is a repetitive list a careful editor would have cut.
what it means: the repetition is the point: each person's identical gift is honored in full.
what a scholar hears: Nachmanides on Numbers 7:2 reads the repetition as equal honor; a midrash gives each identical gift its own tribal meaning.

notes: Numbers 7 paraphrased. The gift list is simplified (the burnt, sin and peace offerings include several animals; the script names them loosely).
Numbers 7 as the longest chapter in the Torah (89 verses): widely stated; confirm.
Ramban's comment on the repetition: confirm the verse he comments on (7:2 or 7:12).
Numbers Rabbah 13–14 gives each tribe's identical offering a different symbolic meaning; confirm.
Nasi from n-s-a is standard; the link to naso is stated plainly.
